In the Miwok word there is one syllable which bears a fixed stress that is not lost or appreciably diminished in connected speech. The stressed syllable is always either the first or second syllable of the word, and is always long. If the first syllable of a word is long, it is always stressed. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: One fixed major stress per word, confined to the first two syllables and always on a LONG syllable (p.6: LONG = long vowel, or short vowel + long consonant or + two consonants). If the first syllable is long it is stressed, even when the second is long too; in words of three or more syllables with a short first syllable the second syllable is long and stressed. Disyllabic stems with no intrinsically long syllable have no major stress: spoken alone they take a secondary stress on the last syllable, in connected speech either syllable or neither is stressed. Hayes 1995:112-113 (on-disk excerpt) reads this as left-edge iambs with final extrametricality and no degenerate feet.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §7.2 pp.7-8: 'Secondary stresses occur, and in short phrases and conversational sentences they are quite noticeable, but they tend..' (continuation not in any snippet); p.8: 'In the longer verb forms there is usually a secondary stress on the final syllable if it is a syllabic pronominal suffix, but if..'; p.8 lists suffixes carrying secondary stress ('.. usitative, and -tàni-, to try to do. hóteţi?-ani-?màš we knelt down; but, hóteţi-ani-š he knelt down. náy-i-iši-nì? he used to scold you; but náy-i?-ìši-? he used to scold.'). Positional/morphological, hedged with 'usually'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stems with no intrinsically long syllable (short-first disyllables such as ?ama? 'grandmother', šalà? 'feather', halè? 'wilderness', nakè? 'end') carry no fixed stress; in isolation a secondary stress on the last syllable, in connected speech 'either syllable may be stressed, or the word may be entirely without stress'; 'Quite frequently the first syllable is stressed in speech, even though the second syllable may be lengthened by some consonantal suffix'. p.11 mentions derivational 'shift of stress and syllabic length' (kalan- 'to dance' -> ká-lan-teyni- 'to dance around').
new_statements.identity_note: Freeland 1951 describes Sierra Miwok with Central, Northern and Southern dialect material; the §7 stress statement is phrased for 'the Miwok word' generally, and the Glottolog reference (17832) files the grammar under Central Sierra Miwok, as does Hayes 1995:112 ('Central Sierra Miwok (§6.3.9)'). Hayes 1995:113 cites Broadbent 1964:17-18 on intonation in 'closely related Southern Sierra Miwok' for the isolation-form secondary stress. Hamp 1966 'Studies in Sierra Miwok' (WALS code mcs, iso csm = Central Sierra Miwok) was not opened.
